messages.subject: Assistance on State-Space Model Issue
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

While fitting a state-space model to mammal fossil data from the Paleobiology Database, I encountered an issue that I haven’t been able to resolve. During simulations ranging from complete to no overlap of covariates in the models for $\phi_t$ and $\gamma_t$, I found that while the model successfully recovers $\gamma_t$, $\phi_t$, and $p_t$, it struggles to recover the intercepts and regression coefficients for both $\gamma_t$ and $\phi_t$.

Below is a figure (with a caption) showing the simulation results for a model with complete covariate overlap. Suspecting potential redundancy between $\gamma_t$ and $\phi_t$, I also tried using an autologistic model with a single parameter $\delta_t$ to summarize the dynamics, but this didn’t improve the results.

I won't include code in this email, but you can find a link to my study page below, which provides more context, a detailed description, figures, and the code itself.

I have a few questions:
Has anyone encountered a similar issue before?
Could this problem be due to my use of a Bernoulli-Binomial mixture to model occupancy and detection? Might it be a case of local (rather than global) identifiability, or could it simply be an unnoticed coding error (if you have the time and interest to check)?
Are there any references or papers presenting simulations using this mixture model with covariates? I haven’t been able to find any.

Any insights would be greatly appreciated!

Have a nice weekend.

Best regards,

André

messages.body_plain:
Just coded up your model in Nimble and it seems to work fine (with 1 simulation).

You can have the Nimble code if you are interested in learning more.

#===============
# Simulate data
#===============
library(boot)

n_spp <- 200  # Number of genera
n_bins <- 30   # Number of time bins
n_surveys <- 10  # Number of surveys (geological formations) per time bin

# Initial occupancy probability
initial_psi <- 0.3

# Detection probability
p <- runif(n_bins,0,1)

# covariate effect on origination
intercept_gamma <- logit(0.2)
beta_gamma1 <- 0.5
beta_gamma2 <- 1

# covariate effect on persistence
intercept_phi <- logit(0.3)
beta_phi1 <- 1
beta_phi2 <- -1

# covariates (generate just once and save to be used in the other two simulation sets)
X1 <- runif (n_bins-1, -2, 2)
X2 <- runif (n_bins-1, -2, 2)

phi <- gamma <- array(NA, dim = (n_bins-1)) # persistence, colonisation

# produce transition probs
for(t in 1:(n_bins-1)){

  # origination
  gamma[t] <- inv.logit(intercept_gamma + beta_gamma1 * X1[t] + beta_gamma2 * X2[t])

  # persistence probability
  phi[t] <- inv.logit(intercept_phi + beta_phi1 * X1[t] + beta_phi2 * X2[t])

} # t

# Simulate occupancy states
z <- array(NA, dim = c(n_spp, n_bins))
muZ <- array(NA, dim = c(n_spp, n_bins-1))
z[,1] <- rbinom(n_spp, 1, initial_psi)

# true incidence
for (i in 1:n_spp) {
  for (t in 2:n_bins) {
    muZ[i,t-1] <- z[i,t-1] * phi[t-1] + (1 - z[i,t-1]) * gamma[t-1]
    z[i,t] <- rbinom(1, 1, muZ[i,t-1])
  } # t
} # i

# Simulate detections
y <- array(NA, dim = c(n_spp, n_bins))
for (i in 1:n_spp) {
  for (t in 1:n_bins) {

    y[i,t] <- rbinom(1, n_surveys, z[i,t] * p[t])

  } # t
} # i

#========================
# Define model in Nimble
#========================
library(nimble)

code <- nimbleCode({

  # Priors
  initial_psi ~ dunif(0,1)
  intercept_gamma ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)
  beta_gamma1 ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)
  beta_gamma2 ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)
  intercept_phi ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)
  beta_phi1 ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)
  beta_phi2 ~ dnorm(0, sd=10)
  for (t in 1:n_bins) {
    p[t] ~ dunif(0,1)
  }

  # Process
  for (t in 1:(n_bins-1)){

    # speciation
    logit(gamma[t]) <-  intercept_gamma +
                        beta_gamma1 * X1[t]+
                        beta_gamma2 * X2[t]

    # persistence
    logit(phi[t]) <-  intercept_phi +
                      beta_phi1 * X1[t]+
                      beta_phi2 * X2[t]

  } # t

  for (g in 1:n_spp) {

    z[g,1] ~ dbern(initial_psi) # occupancy status initialization

    for (t in 2:n_bins){

      muZ[g,t-1] <- z[g,t-1] * phi[t-1] + (1 - z[g,t-1]) * gamma[t-1]
      z[g,t] ~ dbern(muZ[g,t-1])

    }#t

  } #g

  # Observation
  for (g in 1:n_spp) { ## loop over genera

    for (t in 1:n_bins) { ## loop over time bins

      y[g,t] ~ dbin(z[g,t] * p[t], n_surveys)

    } # t

  } # g

}) # nimbleCode

#============
# Run Nimble
#============
# Data
constants <- list(
  n_spp=n_spp, n_bins=n_bins, n_surveys=n_surveys,
  X1=X1, X2=X2
)

data <- list(
  y=y
)

# Initial values
inits <- list(initial_psi=0.5,
              intercept_gamma=0, beta_gamma1=0, beta_gamma2=0,
              intercept_phi=0, beta_phi1=0, beta_phi2=0,
              p=rep(0.5,n_bins), z=ifelse(y==0,0,1)
)

start_time <- Sys.time() # start time of computing

model <- nimbleModel(code, constants=constants, data=data, inits=inits)
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(model)
mcmcConf$printSamplers()

mcmc <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
compiled <- compileNimble(model, mcmc)

fit <- runMCMC(compiled$mcmc, nchains = 3, niter = 5000, nburnin = 0)

end_time <- Sys.time() # end time of computing
time_taken <- end_time - start_time # computing time
time_taken

#===============
# Check results
#===============
parms <- c('initial_psi', 'intercept_gamma', 'beta_gamma1', 'beta_gamma2', 'intercept_phi', 'beta_phi1', 'beta_phi2')
parm_values <- c(initial_psi, intercept_gamma, beta_gamma1, beta_gamma2, intercept_phi, beta_phi1, beta_phi2)
fitnms <- colnames(fit$chain1)

library(rstan)

par(mfrow=c(3,3))
par(mar=c(2,2,2,1))
for (i in 1:length(parms)) {
  tt <- cbind(fit$chain1[,which(fitnms == parms[i])],
              fit$chain2[,which(fitnms == parms[i])],
              fit$chain3[,which(fitnms == parms[i])])
  diff <- max(abs(tt[2001:5000,] - parm_values[i])) * 1.2
  plot(1, xlim=c(1,5000), ylim=c(parm_values[i]-diff,parm_values[i]+diff),
       type='n', xlab='', ylab='', main=parms[i])
  for (k in 1:3) {
    lines(tt[,k], type='l', col=k+1)
  } # k
  abline(h=parm_values[i], col='grey20')
  text(x=3000, y=parm_values[i]+diff, pos=1,
       labels=paste(c('Rhat = ', format(round(Rhat(tt[2001:5000,]), digits=2), nsmall=2)), collapse=''))
} # i

messages.subject: Occupancy model for nomadic species
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am interested in understanding the occupancy patterns of a nomadic species that move throughout the landscape, presumably given seasonal food availability. To capture these patterns, we are collecting monthly presence/absence data across all known roosting sites. The end goal is to understand the seasonal probability of occupancy across the region and investigate how different factors might explain some of these dynamics. This will hopefully provide a clearer picture of how these species use the landscape, which will be important for effective management.

I was wondering what the best approach to analysing this type of data would be if the species were intermittently present in an area. It would be important to understand whether the species was truly absent in an area or just went undetected at that particular time, so my default option was using some sort of dynamics occupancy model. However, this is the first time I have worked in a system like this, so I was hoping someone with more experience could point me in the right direction.

Thank you for your time.

All my best,

Alejandro

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alejandro,

Traditional dynamic occupancy models require repeat sampling within periods of assumed closure. Say, every month you did a few surveys that were close together in time to estimate the occupancy for that particular month. In the absence of repeat surveys, say you just do one survey per month to inform the occupancy of that month, the model is not or weakly identified. If, on the other hand, you have something like automated recording units (ARUs) like SongMeters, then it becomes a lot easier to look at fine-grained site usage such as seasonal occupancy. What sort of data are you working with? That will help us to inform on a good model.

Cheers,

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> Would dynamic occupancy models be able to capture the probability that the species has left, returned, or continuously stayed at each location for each month during the study period?

Short answer, yes. For each primary occasion (month in this case) you can get a posterior distribution for that site's occupancy state. If you're using maximum likelihood or the latent states are marginalised out in a Bayesian framework, you can still recover these. So yes, you will be able to make probabilistic claims about when sites were occupied.

>  Assuming that dynamic occupancy models are the best tool to understand these nomadic dynamics, would you recommend we incorporate a more robust design with, say, three visits within a week (when we assume closure) and repeat this every month (when we assume that the species might or might not have left the location)?

Yes. But if detection probability is really high, as in you'll basically certainly detect the species if it's present, then this is unnecessary. In this case, you can just use the results of single surveys as an indicator for occupancy.

>  These species live in large groups, so population closure in terms of number of individuals is uncertain (we are unsure if all individuals return to the same roost after foraging).

Yeah, closure here just refers to the occupancy state, so that the occupancy state doesn't change between your secondary surveys. If you were also interested in modeling latent abundance, something like an N-mixture model might work as well. But again, if detection probabilities are quite high, you might not even have to account for imperfect detection.

Cheers,

Matt

messages.subject_clean: How to fit occupancy models to camtrap data ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've had a colleague visiting who has camera-trap data and wants to fit occupancy models to learn about determinants of habitat use and possibly make distribution maps. I don't know much about how to do occupancy modeling with camtrap data, so I am reaching out to this group.

The data are for 5 species, over about 12 years, in an area of perhaps 1000 km2 and are extremely sparse: e.g., there are only 90 trap locations in total, and the data are extremely imbalanced. In one year there was never any trap deployed and in most years there are only a couple dozen at best. The total number of days with detections ranges from 69 in the most-commonly detected species to about 12 in the least commonly detected.

Many traps seem to have been running for several months and so I suggested grouping the data into intervals of at least one week each. In part to reduce temporal autocorrelation in detection, which can be problematic according to the  recent paper by Goldstein <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.14359> et al.

My main question to this group is about how to discretize space. That is, what is a "site" ? On the one extreme, one might treat each camtrap location as a site, but then one would have very non-independent sites, and (given the spread of the camtraps) the occupancy estimate would then have a very extreme interpretation as "probability of use", rather than as probability of "permanent presence" (since most of the species would then likely have some individuals detected at more than one trap).

On the other hand, one might treat as sites grid cells of, say, 4, 16, 25, ..., 100 square kilometers. Often, people seem to choose a grid cell size that is approximately equal to the homerange of a study species.

Thanks for any comments on this, or for hints at useful papers.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc and all--

The question "what is a site" has given me a lot of confusion in past work with occupancy models + camera traps. My preferred approach has been to define a "site" at the camera level and interpret the estimated occupancy probability as the probability that the area surveyed by the camera was used by at least one individual of the species of interest during the camera's deployment. I think of this as an "asymptotic" occupancy probability following Efford and Dawson <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/ES11-00308.1>. Discretizing space could be useful for defining the scale at which the occupancy probability is calculated, but I have the feeling that it wouldn't necessarily be meaningful for defining latent states that are shared between cameras. Then you'd end up with an asymptotic occupancy probability that I'd interpret as the probability that an animal uses at least one camera in the spatial unit at least once.

To me there are two big outstanding questions with the above, regardless of how sites are defined, which are (1) what is the spatial scale at which the "site use" of the area sampled by a camera varies (related to animal movement), and (2) does "rate of site use" actually tell us anything meaningful about biology? Per #2, there's some good recent work arguing that camera-level "occupancy" is not actually correlated with density, especially when individual animal movement rates vary (Parsons et al. <https://academic.oup.com/jmammal/article/98/6/1547/4430381>; Steenweg et al. <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ecy.2054>; Stauffer et al. <https://wildlife.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jwmg.22105>).

A group I collaborate with has a review paper coming out any day now where we give our thoughts on some issues related to animal movement, occupancy, detection, and density. I'll link to it in this thread once it's published.

I definitely recommend wide temporal intervals for your discrete detection histories!

Best,
Ben

Hi all,

Marc, I've been working on an occupancy model approach for passive acoustic recorders which would also work for camera traps. The likelihood is defined here <https://github.com/jsocolar/flocker/issues/105#issuecomment-2381256842> and it pretty well aligns with what you said: the idea is to split the deployment period into shorter occasions within which you're willing to assume closure, then occupancy and detection is estimated for each occasion. One of the things that makes it identified is that you often get multiple detections within a period so you can use a continuous time formulation (either exponential with something like a Hawkes process to account for non-independence) or Poisson.

Cheers,

Matt

Hi Marc,

The spOccupancy package has been a game changer for us.  We've been monitoring wildlife occupancy across 40,000 km2 of the Canadian Rockies for the last twelve years with variable camera trap effort in some regions.  As you know, the spOccupancy functions can incorporate temporal and spatial autocorrelation and the resulting maps for spatial predictions of annual occupancy and changes in occupancy look much more reasonable compared to predictions that ignore spatial autocorrelation.

Spatially imbalanced study designs can also affect the interpretation of occupancy when summarised across a study.  For that reason, I currently predict occupancy (use) for a grid of cells across the study area and summarise occupancy based on those gridded predictions rather than predictions for each camera site.

Ben raises a good point about occupancy-abundance relationships.  Interestingly, we found that declining trends for wolverine density and occupancy were highly correlated within our study area.  Barrueto et al 2022 <https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-21499-4>.

Jesse Whittington
Wildlife Ecologist
Banff National Park
